newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey risks inflation from dollar-linked wages.
newsitem.headline: Turkey risks inflation from dollar-linked wages.

text.p: Economists said on Wednesday Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's plan for indexing public sector wages to the dollar was a dangerous game which could send the country's economy into an inflationary spiral.

"A country should not enter into such an indexation. If it enters, it can't come out of it easily. This puts the economy into an inflationary spiral," said Faruk Selcuk, an associate professor of economics at Ankara's Bilkent University.

Despite Erbakan's remarks late on Tuesday that wages of public employees would be adjusted to remain constant in dollar terms next year, the Islamist-led coalition government seems to be at odds on the plan.
State Minister Ufuk Soylemez, a cabinet member from the coalition's centre-right partner True Path Party (DYP), said a dollar-indexed wage rise is out of the question.

"The increase...in civil servant salaries will not remain below inflation. The inflation target (for 1997) is 65 percent and growth target is four percent. We propose a rise of 65, plus four percent," he told Reuters.
However economists remain cautious.

"What the Prime Minister has said is very clear. He clearly means that wages are to be indexed to foreign currencies," said a senior private bank economist. "Under such a system, inflation will feed itself."
The economist said any indexation of salaries to the dollar would weaken the ground for implementation of a stability programme, firmly urged by businessmen and western financial institutions.
Bureaucrats in charge of the economy say Erbakan's plan would be hard to apply.

They say the government is likely to continue to hold pay rises on par with inflation for the coming months. Turkey has been trying to depreciate its currency in line with inflation in the past two years as part of its monetary policy.
Some private sector companies have already indexed wages to the dollar and many landlords charge rental fees on a dollar-basis or simply in dollars.
Many Turks lend in dollar terms instead of the Turkish lira to hedge against chronic inflation, running at around 80 percent.
Economists say dollar-indexed wages will erode what little credibility the Turkish lira retains.
"You can never lower inflation unless you remove indexation to the dollar in the economy," Selcuk said.

The conflicting remarks by Erbakan and Soylemez reveal fundamental differences between the pro-market and western economic policies of deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller's DYP and populist and anti-western policies of Erbakan's Islamist Welfare Party.

"Erbakan's party is not well-prepared to govern the economy. Sometimes he is coming up with very lose and vague remarks about the economy and pushing the markets into a wave of uncertainty," the private bank economist said.
Earlier this week a report in the mass-circulation daily Hurriyet that Erbakan had asked the Treasury to halt domestic borrowing sharply pulled depressed t-bill yields on the bond market.

Erbakan neither confirmed nor denied the report but the rates recovered after his coalition partner, Ciller, assured the market that domestic borrowing would continue in line with the cash needs of the Treasury.

The discord between the Welfare and the DYP on economic policies is also expected to surface during possible talks with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for a new stand-by arrangement later this year.

The coalition's DYP wing urges the government to reach an accord with the IMF. Welfare, on the other hand, has emerged as a leading opponent of any deal with the IMF, World Bank and European Union in the past decade.
